cim: Economic Frameworks Clarify Open Risk Standards Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act
cim_eredeti: Economic Frameworks Clarify Open Risk Standards Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act
szoveg_eredeti:
Economic Frameworks Clarify Open Risk Standards Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act

A legal and economic analysis published in Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance demonstrates that the implementation of artificial intelligence governance under the European Union AI Act requires an external economic framework to transform indeterminate statutory terms into an actionable standard of care. Enacted as a central pillar of European digital regulation, Article 9 of the AI Act mandates that providers of high-risk artificial intelligence systems establish, implement, document, and maintain continuous risk management systems. However, the legal text relies on fundamentally open-ended terminology, requiring organizations to identify known and reasonably foreseeable risks under Article 9(2)(a) and implement targeted measures until overall residual risks are judged acceptable under Article 9(5). Without an objective methodology to evaluate these provisions, regulatory enforcement risks either imposing excessive precautionary requirements that stifle technological innovation or permitting overly permissive practices that compromise public health, safety, and fundamental rights. The study shows that theoretical models derived from unilateral tort law and economic analysis offer the necessary analytical structure to balance these competing societal priorities effectively.

The study examines the significant structural transformations that Article 9 underwent during the legislative negotiations leading from the European Commission’s original 2021 proposal to the final compromise text. The initial draft established an exceptionally rigid standard, requiring providers to identify all foreseeable risks without regard to the reasonableness of the investigative burden and compelling the elimination or reduction of risks as far as possible under the strict as-far-as-possible principle. In contrast, the finalized legislation replaced these unyielding requirements with a explicit reasonableness threshold for risk discovery and abandoned the as-far-as-possible mandate in favor of requiring appropriate measures that eliminate or reduce hazards in as far as technically feasible through system design and development. While the European Parliament unsuccessfully sought to introduce an explicit reasonableness qualification into Article 9(5), the finalized statutory wording departed completely from existing risk management concepts in sector-specific European Union legislation such as the Medical Device Regulation. This legislative evolution created an undefined standard that deliberately opened the regulatory framework to economic interpretation.

By drawing upon long-standing theoretical parallels between product liability, tort law, and industrial risk governance, the research paper demonstrates how unilateral tort models directly operationalize the statutory duty of care. In conventional economic models of tort law, rational actors are obligated to invest in precautionary measures only up to the point where the marginal cost of taking additional precautions equals the marginal benefit achieved through risk reduction. The study establishes that this marginal balancing directly mirrors established regulatory frameworks in capital-intensive sectors, such as maritime safety standards enforced by the European Maritime Safety Agency and probabilistic risk management provisions governing the nuclear energy industry. Under this economic reading of Article 9, identifying risks and deploying mitigations represent operational costs of precaution, whereas the legal definition of risk under Article 3(2)—defined as the combination of the probability of harm and the severity of that harm—means that regulatory benefits correspond to the verifiable reduction in expected negative impacts achieved by design alterations.

Applying this marginal cost-benefit framework to the initial obligation of risk discovery resolves the ambiguity surrounding the undefined statutory benchmark of reasonably foreseeable risks. In both common law traditions and continental civil law systems, legal reasonableness is anchored in the standard of care expected from a prudent, cautious, and well-informed average practitioner conducting risk management. The economic interpretation demonstrates that an artificial intelligence provider fulfills this obligation when it pursues all risk identification procedures whose marginal cost remains below the expected marginal informational benefit of uncovering potential hazards. When the cost of further exploration exceeds the expected marginal benefit, requiring additional open-ended investigations becomes economically unreasonable. Because investigating previously unobserved vulnerabilities is inherently an exploratory endeavor where severe risks may hypothetically appear with miniscule probability, a strict marginal test prevents organizations from being forced into wasteful, exhaustive searches that offer negligible societal protection while halting developmental pipelines.

The analysis extends this economic reasoning to Article 9(5) by formulating a structured two-step evaluation test to determine whether residual risks can legitimately be judged acceptable. The first analytical step obligates the provider to execute a standard marginal cost-benefit calculation that explicitly incorporates the opportunity costs generated when risk mitigation measures degrade the computational speed, functional capabilities, or overall utility of the high-risk system. Precautionary measures must be instituted whenever the marginal expenditure is lower than the societal benefit derived from the corresponding risk reduction. The second step introduces an overarching risk-utility balancing mechanism, directly inspired by European product safety rules found in Annex I of both the Medical Device Regulation and the In-Vitro-Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation. Under this second-step review, residual risks that would otherwise appear marginally elevated may be judged legally acceptable if the high-risk system delivers exceptionally high societal utility, such as specialized diagnostic healthcare software, whereas systems offering minimal societal benefits face far more stringent acceptability thresholds.

Despite the mathematical precision offered by quantitative economic modeling, the research paper proves that a purely quantitative approach to artificial intelligence risk management is technically unviable and substantively inadequate. In practice, full quantification routinely fails because developers lack standardized, context-specific performance datasets and validated technical metrics across complex operational environments. More critically, high-risk systems under the AI Act directly interface with human dignity, non-discrimination, privacy, and other fundamental rights protected under the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. These fundamental constitutional rights embody deeply normative, qualitative, and value-laden trade-offs that cannot be translated into uniform mathematical values or automated formulas. For instance, optimizing algorithmic fairness metrics to eliminate demographic discrimination frequently requires ingesting and processing expanded categories of sensitive personal data, thereby creating unavoidable systemic conflicts with fundamental privacy and data minimization principles that can only be resolved through deliberate human value judgments rather than algorithmic calculations.

A further critical limitation of unconstrained quantification identified in the study is the acute vulnerability of numerical compliance frameworks to strategic corporate manipulation, characterized as metrics shopping or fairness hacking.
